CAPCOM PLANS TO USE AI TO SPEED UP THE GAME DEVELOPMENT PROCESS
articles.summary: Capcom intends to use AI to speed up game development through REX, a major overhaul of its RE Engine meant to create a "game engine of the AI generation." Programmer Satoshi Ishida said AI would mainly streamline workflows, since larger games and assets have lengthened development times. Capcom had earlier said AI would assist with graphics, sound and programming, while AI-generated content would stay out of its games.

articles.title: REDESIGNED MACBOOK PRO WITH OLED TO FEATURE ‘SIGNIFICANTLY LIGHTER' DESIGN
articles.summary: Apple's upcoming MacBook Pro redesign will reportedly be significantly lighter thanks to miniaturized parts and a rearranged internal architecture, addressing the substantial weight of current models, particularly the 16-inch version. The overhaul is also expected to introduce Tandem OLED displays, touchscreens, and a Dynamic Island, with macOS Golden Gate receiving changes to support the new interactions. The M5 Pro and M5 Max models are expected to launch by November, as Apple reportedly skips higher-end M6 chips to accelerate its transition to M7.

articles.title: OPENAI IS ADDING INVISIBLE WATERMARKS TO CHATGPT AND CODEX FOR USERS IN THE EU
articles.summary: OpenAI will begin adding invisible, machine-readable watermarks called textGrain to eligible ChatGPT and Codex output in the EU to comply with transparency requirements in the EU AI Act. The technology embeds a statistical pattern into generated language rather than adding hidden characters. API customers worldwide can optionally enable it for supported models. OpenAI acknowledges that watermarking remains imperfect because editing and short outputs can weaken the detectable signal.

articles.title: DESIGNING FOR PEOPLE WHO ARE COLOR BLIND
articles.summary: Color blindness affects about one in 12 men and one in 200 women, making key information, interactive elements, and color-coded data harder to perceive. Designs should pair color with an icon, pattern, or text label per WCAG 1.4.1, keep sufficient contrast, and avoid red-green and purple-blue pairings. Blue is a safer hue, though not guaranteed. Grayscale checks help, and hover, focus, and disabled states need non-color cues, ideally tested with real people.

articles.title: DESIGNING FOR VOICE FIRST
articles.summary: Designing a voice-first app is hard because touch-and-typing workflows get decided first, leaving speech as another way to fill in the same fields. Five principles guide it: make spoken context count, let people steer as they think, show understanding, make correction easy, and let attention come and go. Voice should survive the shift from desk to AirPods and dog walks, so a returning user sees what happened and what still needs them.

articles.title: AI INVASIVE DESIGN
articles.summary: Treating “AI native” as a mandate to maximize AI usage risks replacing valuable existing interactions simply to make products appear technologically current. A better approach treats human behavior as the ecosystem and asks AI to fit naturally within it by reflecting intent, providing adaptable scaffolding, maintaining consistent mental models, and scaling work without overwhelming people. Successful AI products should also preserve human participation and skills, because excessive automation can erode motivation, competence, and the value users get from doing meaningful work themselves.

articles.title: YOU CAN'T DESCRIBE YOUR WAY TO GREAT DESIGN
articles.summary: Prompt-driven AI tools force creative work into a describe-generate-evaluate loop that poorly supports the instinctive experimentation and continuous manipulation involved in serious design. Current tools tend to offer either editable but constrained output or expressive but largely fixed results, leaving professionals without the combination of creative range and direct control they need. Better AI creative tools should behave more like canvases where people can manipulate generated material fluidly, preserve editability, explore alternatives, and remain actively involved in shaping the work.

articles.title: WHAT THE 500 IN BLUE-500 MEANS
articles.summary: Numbers in color scales such as blue-500 may look standardized, but different design systems use them to represent entirely different concepts, including position in a ramp, guaranteed contrast relationships, measured lightness, or semantic roles. Material Design's original 50–900 scale primarily described positions and established 500 as a typical primary color, while systems such as Carbon, Material 3, and Radix give their numbers more explicit meaning. Understanding what a scale actually encodes is important because two colors carrying the same numerical label can have very different lightness, contrast, and intended uses.
